text: We built the same lookup-a-price procedure in T-SQL and PL/SQL last lesson. Now let's finish the set with MySQL and PostgreSQL — two platforms that each add their own real wrinkle to the pattern, one a syntax quirk, one a genuine piece of platform history.

MySQL first. Delimiter slash slash, create procedure get product price, in p underscore product id int, out p underscore price decimal ten two, begin, select list price into p underscore price from products where product id equals p underscore product id, end slash slash, delimiter semicolon. That delimiter dance at the top and bottom isn't decoration — the procedure body itself is full of ordinary semicolons, so without temporarily changing the terminator, the MySQL client would think the very first semicolon inside the body ends the whole create procedure statement. This course's MySQL chapter covers delimiter in more depth; here, just know why it's there.

Calling it: call get product price open paren seven oh seven comma at result price close paren, then select at result price. Two things to notice — MySQL uses call, not exec, and the output value lands in an at-prefixed session variable, not a locally declared one.

PostgreSQL has a genuinely interesting history here. For most of its life, Postgres had no create procedure at all — only create function, and developers used functions for everything, even operations that were really side-effecting. Real procedures only arrived in PostgreSQL eleven, back in twenty eighteen. Create or replace procedure get product price, p underscore product id int, inout p underscore price numeric ten two, as dollar dollar, begin, select list price into p underscore price, end, dollar dollar language plpgsql. Notice inout is one word here, not the two-word in out you saw in PL/SQL.

Calling it: do dollar dollar, declare v underscore result price numeric, begin, call get product price open paren seven oh seven comma v underscore result price close paren, raise notice, end dollar dollar. Same call keyword as MySQL — and unlike a plain PostgreSQL function, which you'd just call inside a select, a real procedure needs that call keyword explicitly.

So: MySQL needs delimiter because its body is full of semicolons, and PostgreSQL's real create procedure is younger than you might assume — anything written before twenty eighteen built everything as a function instead. Next lesson, we look at functions themselves across all four platforms, including a real limitation worth remembering: MySQL has no table-valued function concept at all. See you there.
